“The stars are lovely tonight,” the mason agreed. “So many of them are out.”

“And look at the moon!” cried the queen. “It’s the most beautiful it’s been all winter.”

The king and queen stepped off the ladder, and the mason continued to the moon’s surface. He set his tool box down and opened it. He selected a hammer and a piece of metal netting and got to work.

As he worked, he could see the royal couple talking in whispers below. He turned back to his work.

Minutes passed, then hours.

The mason stood up and stretched. He lifted his tools and moon-glass fragments into his toolbox. He checked his work, unable to find any flaws.

Satisfied, he closed the box, clipped it to his belt, and hopped onto the ladder.

On his way down, he passed an old man.

“What’s it like, being so high up?” the old man asked, looking at the moon.

“The stars are very bright up there,” the mason said. “And you can see how the little things fit together. I can fix the big cracks, but I can still see how the smaller ones fit into them. They’re part of the whole. And that makes the work easier.”

The old man smiled. “Thanks for fixing the moon.”

The mason slid down to the ground and unclipped his toolbox. “It was my pleasure,” he told the old man. He hefted the box and walked off towards his home.

He stopped when he was out of the king’s sight and looked up.

What a beautifully reflective observation, and you’re absolutely right. That struggle—the tension between wanting things to be “perfect” and needing to let go and just create—is such an essential, universal part of writing (and of sharing anything, really).

Sometimes, the best ideas come from letting go of a certain part–for example, momentarily dropping the desire for the “perfect ending.” A cliffhanger, an unresolved moment, a slightly awkward line—these sometimes resonate more than something over-polished. They’re honest in their messiness. 

What’s also powerful is looking back at earlier drafts and seeing how your own thoughts and style have changed. Those iterations are proof of growth, and sometimes the most compelling stories come from the sparks of unfinished business you leave behind—the questions, the abrupt shifts, the unwanted endings.

Your advice about not chasing perfection rings true. Creation is a process, a dialogue with yourself (and your audience). Sometimes the world you build will hold more meaning in its imperfections, its abandoned corners, its rough edges. If you keep iterating endlessly, you might lose the sense of *now*—the moment when something felt true or necessary, even if it was messy.

And that longing for human connection you discovered in your revision—that’s likely more compelling than the disconnected tiredness you first described. It’s alive because it asks something of the reader, rather than just showing.

In other words: Yes, embrace the mess. Let there be unfinished things. Grows come from the cracks as much as from the polished parts.<|endoftext|>

Translated literally, this is a very interesting passage. But as any good deconstructionist will tell you, that’s not what matters. What’s interesting is just how much of it is true.

The moon, and the moon’s apparent size, and the tests regarding perspective that you can execute on the moon.

The moon is made of something, but it’s not glass.

The mason is less of a person and more of a job title.

The cracks in the moon are what’s interesting to me, because there are a lot of things that could be going on there.

Who repaired the moon before the royal mason?

Does the fact that the moon reflects light mean that it’s solid? Are there ‘feeling’ and ‘thoughts’ on the moon, or is it just another ball of rock that gets a lot of attention?

How much does perspective have to do with the moon? Do we, in fact, only see what we want to see? Or do we see the moon as we do because that’s the best we’re capable of with our Earth-bound eyes?

Why? Why is the moon so much brighter than everything else in the night sky? Why does it feel so big?

Can you climb a ladder to the moon? Can you land a spaceship there? Can you get close enough to fix it?

And why would you? How long has the moon been broken?

“You’re the moon.”
“I’m the what?”
“Exactly.”

The moon is beautiful, more beautiful than it’s ever been because it’s broken, and when you stand on top of the moon and look down on all the people who do the same, you realize that everyone is the every one, and that the brightest object in the night sky is still, and always will be, figuratively in every regard, out of everyone’s reach.

Days—or years?—him in solitude, the mason’s thoughts become seeds that twist and sprout in the dark. Sometimes he dreams of the glittering rain of glass shards, of the woman’s voice like silver bells, and always of her eyes—eyes he never saw.

One long night, as the rain raps against his cell, still damp with the glimmer of moonlight, the door groans open. She stands there, silhouette edged in radiant white, shield left forgotten at her feet. The woman looks older now, older and sadder. But her hair still shines like midnight snow.

He throws himself against his cot, back to the wall.

“To sentence a man to death and yet grant him life? What are you?”

She steps forward quietly—too lightly for the earth, too strongly for a dream. In the gray light he sees that her hands, slimmer and shakier than he remembered, bear kind old scars and blisters.

“My name is Madeline,” she says softly. “Ten and twenty winters. Once, I was the Moon Knight, as my city called me. My shield protected them from real dangers, and from nightmares.”

He listens, heart hammering.

“You shattered the glass moon, Madeline. Why? Are you the L MDB they mumble of in prison halls?”

She hesitates, voice a thread of moonlight. “I am the Living Dreammind Breaker. I could mend hearts. Or, when they cracked, I took them apart. But I was tired. Of hiding behind shining shields and polished masks. Of never being seen—me, not the moon.”

He ventures from his cot. “You sentenced me to death. Why let me live?”

She almost laughs. “Perhaps I wanted you to see me, not my mask. Or perhaps…” Her eyes drop. “Perhaps I wanted mercy for myself.”

He steps closer. “Did you?”

“That night, in the tower, I meant to let you go. But your words—” She pauses. “What did you say to me then, before the glass fell?”
